title: 11 — Pipeline Patterns and Practices
html:
11 — Pipeline Patterns and Practices

The one idea: a production pipeline will be rerun, backfilled, fed duplicates, fed late data and changed by someone else next year. Senior data engineering is designing for those events on day one — incremental, idempotent, parameterised, tested and observable — so that each of them is routine rather than an incident.

1. Incremental processing with high-watermarks

Reprocessing everything every run is simple but gets slower and more expensive as data grows. Incremental processing reads only what is new.

Mechanism Tracks Best for
High-watermark column Max modified_at / sequence id already processed, stored in a control table JDBC sources with a reliable change column
Streaming checkpoint Offsets / files / Delta versions processed Delta, Kafka, Auto Loader sources (preferred when available)
Change Data Feed Delta versions processed Propagating silver changes to gold
Partition-based Which date partitions are complete Daily batch facts

A high-watermark control table pattern:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ops.watermarks (
  pipeline      STRING NOT NULL,
  source_table  STRING NOT NULL,
  watermark     TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at    TIMESTAMP
);

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

PIPELINE, SOURCE = "crm_customers", "dbo.Customers"
OVERLAP = "INTERVAL 10 MINUTES"   # re-read a small window to catch in-flight transactions

wm_row = spark.sql(f"""
  SELECT watermark FROM ops.watermarks
  WHERE pipeline = '{PIPELINE}' AND source_table = '{SOURCE}'
""").first()
low = wm_row["watermark"] if wm_row else None

src = spark.read.format("jdbc").option("url", jdbc_url).option("dbtable", SOURCE).load()
if low is not None:
    src = src.filter(F.col("ModifiedAt") > F.lit(low) - F.expr(OVERLAP))

src = src.cache()
new_wm = src.agg(F.max("ModifiedAt")).first()[0]

if new_wm is not None:
    # 1. Idempotent write first (MERGE keyed on the business key, see §2)
    upsert_customers(src)   # keyed MERGE into silver.customers, defined elsewhere in the job
    # 2. Only then advance the watermark
    spark.sql(f"""
      MERGE INTO ops.watermarks t
      USING (SELECT '{PIPELINE}' AS pipeline, '{SOURCE}' AS source_table,
                    TIMESTAMP'{new_wm}' AS watermark) s
      ON t.pipeline = s.pipeline AND t.source_table = s.source_table
      WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET watermark = s.watermark, updated_at = current_timestamp()
      WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (pipeline, source_table, watermark, updated_at)
                            VALUES (s.pipeline, s.source_table, s.watermark, current_timestamp())
    """)
src.unpersist()

Rules:

  • Write data, then advance the watermark. If the job dies between the two, the next run re-reads a little data, and the idempotent merge absorbs it. The reverse order loses data.
  • Filter pushdown: Spark pushes the ModifiedAt filter into the JDBC query, so the source does the filtering. Make sure the source has an index on the column.
  • Overlap + idempotent write handles transactions that commit after the watermark was read.
  • Where a streaming source exists (Delta, Kafka, files), prefer checkpoints over hand-rolled watermarks.

2. Idempotent writes

Every write should be safe to repeat. Choose by the shape of the data:

Data shape Idempotent write
Entities with a key (customers, orders) MERGE on the key, source deduplicated
Facts for a period (daily sales) Overwrite that period: replaceWhere / INSERT ... REPLACE WHERE
Append-only events with unique IDs MERGE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (insert-only merge) on the event ID
Streaming micro-batch appends Delta streaming sink (exactly-once), or txnAppId/txnVersion inside foreachBatch
Full snapshot of a small table Full overwrite 
-- Insert-only merge: re-delivered events are ignored
MERGE INTO silver.events t
USING new_events s
  ON t.event_id = s.event_id
 AND t.event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 3 DAYS   -- bound the scan to where duplicates can exist
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

The date bound in the ON clause is a performance choice with a correctness trade-off: duplicates older than three days would be inserted again. Pick the bound from how late re-deliveries can realistically arrive.

What breaks idempotency:

  • Blind append of a batch that might be re-run.
  • Using current_timestamp() or now() for business logic (e.g. "orders from the last 24 hours") instead of the logical date parameter.
  • Generating random or sequence IDs during transformation for rows that already exist.
  • Side effects (sending emails, calling APIs) inside transformation code.

3. Deduplication

Duplicates arrive from at-least-once delivery, producer retries, overlapping incremental windows and re-sent files. Deduplicate at two levels:

  1. Within a batch: keep one row per key.
  2. Against the target: do not insert a key that already exists (merge).
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

w = (Window.partitionBy("event_id")
     .orderBy(F.col("event_time").desc(), F.col("_ingested_at").desc()))

deduped = (batch
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
    .filter("rn = 1")
    .drop("rn"))

Choose the key carefully:

  • A producer-generated event ID is best.
  • If there is none, a hash of the business-relevant columns (sha2(concat_ws('||', ...), 256)) — but be sure two genuinely distinct events can never produce identical content.
  • For Kafka, (topic, partition, offset) identifies a message, which dedupes re-reads but not producer retries that wrote the same event twice.

Always use a deterministic tie-breaker in the ORDER BY. With ties, row_number() can pick different rows on different runs, making the pipeline non-deterministic.

4. Late and out-of-order data

Where Technique
Streaming aggregations Watermark sized from the measured lateness distribution
Entity upserts Sequence guard in MERGE: only apply a change if s.change_ts > t.change_ts
Daily batch facts Reprocess a rolling window (e.g. the last 3 days) each run with partition overwrite
Dimensions arriving after facts Inferred member rows, updated when the real dimension arrives
Very late corrections Scheduled correction job that recomputes affected partitions from silver 
---
title: Rolling reprocessing window for late data
---
flowchart LR
    R["Daily run for D"] --> W["Recompute partitions<br/>D-2, D-1, D"]
    W --> O["Overwrite exactly those<br/>partitions (replaceWhere)"]
    O --> C["Late events for D-2 and D-1<br/>now included, nothing duplicated"]

from datetime import date, timedelta
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

run_date = date.fromisoformat(dbutils.widgets.get("run_date"))
start = run_date - timedelta(days=2)

daily = (spark.table("silver.sales")
    .filter(F.col("sale_date").between(F.lit(start), F.lit(run_date)))
    .groupBy("sale_date", "store_id")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))

(daily.write.format("delta")
    .mode("overwrite")
    .option("replaceWhere", f"sale_date BETWEEN '{start}' AND '{run_date}'")
    .saveAsTable("gold.daily_store_sales"))

Communicate this to consumers: "yesterday's number can still change for 2 days" is a legitimate contract, as long as it is stated.

5. Backfills without double counting

A backfill is safe if and only if the job is idempotent per slice. Checklist:

  1. The job takes a date (or range) parameter and processes exactly that slice.
  2. The write replaces exactly that slice (replaceWhere) or merges by key.
  3. Upstream data for the slice exists — backfilling gold from a silver table that only holds 90 days will silently produce zeros for older dates.
  4. Run slices in parallel with a concurrency limit, so you do not overwhelm the source or the cluster; slices must not overlap (overlapping replaceWhere writes conflict).
  5. Reconcile afterwards: row counts and totals per slice vs source.
  6. Snapshot before: note the table version so you can RESTORE if the backfill is wrong.
# Driving a backfill through a job's for-each task or a simple loop
import datetime as dt

days = [dt.date(2026, 1, 1) + dt.timedelta(d) for d in range(0, 90)]
for d in days:
    dbutils.notebook.run("./daily_sales", timeout_seconds=3600, arguments={"run_date": d.isoformat()})

(A job's for-each task can run the iterations in parallel with a configured concurrency, which is preferable to a sequential notebook loop.)

Anti-pattern: a backfill script separate from the daily job. Two code paths drift apart, and the backfilled history no longer matches what the daily job would have produced.

6. SCD2 end to end

---
title: SCD2 dimension pipeline end to end
---
flowchart LR
    SRC["CRM database"] -->|"log-based CDC"| BR["bronze.crm_customers_cdc<br/>append-only change events"]
    BR -->|"dedupe, type, validate"| SV["silver.customers<br/>current state (SCD1 merge)"]
    BR -->|"ordered changes"| D2["gold.dim_customer<br/>SCD2 history"]
    D2 --> F["gold.fact_sales<br/>lookup surrogate key<br/>valid at sale time"]

Steps:

  1. Bronze: append raw change events with op, change_ts (source commit time or log sequence number), and ingestion metadata.
  2. Silver current-state table: foreachBatch MERGE with a sequence guard (see chapter 09).
  3. Gold SCD2 dimension: either the two-copy MERGE (see chapter 08) or declarative pipelines' APPLY CHANGES/AUTO CDC with stored_as_scd_type=2, which handles multiple changes per key per batch and out-of-order events.
  4. Fact surrogate key lookup: join facts to the dimension version valid at the event time.
-- Point-in-time surrogate key lookup for facts
SELECT s.sale_id,
       s.sale_ts,
       s.amount,
       COALESCE(d.customer_sk, -1) AS customer_sk      -- -1 = unknown member row
FROM silver.sales s
LEFT JOIN gold.dim_customer d
  ON  s.customer_id = d.customer_id
  AND s.sale_ts >= d.valid_from
  AND s.sale_ts <  d.valid_to;

Decisions to document: which attributes are type 2 vs type 1, whether valid_to is exclusive, the "unknown" member key, and how deletes are represented.

7. CDC ingestion into bronze → silver

---
title: CDC from an OLTP database into the lakehouse
---
flowchart LR
    DB[("SQL Server<br/>transaction log")] --> CDC["CDC connector<br/>(Debezium, managed connector)"]
    CDC --> K["Kafka / Event Hubs<br/>one topic per table"]
    K --> B["Bronze: raw change events<br/>append, keep offsets"]
    B --> S["Silver: MERGE by primary key<br/>ordered by LSN / change_ts"]
    SNAP["Initial snapshot<br/>(bulk load)"] --> B

Things that go wrong, and the fix:

Problem Fix
Initial load and stream overlap or leave a gap Take the snapshot at a known log position, then start CDC from that position; merge with sequence guards so overlap is harmless
Several changes to one key in one micro-batch Deduplicate to the latest by sequence number before MERGE (or apply in order if intermediate versions matter)
Out-of-order events across partitions Partition topics by primary key so one key's changes stay ordered; guard MERGE with sequence comparison
Deletes Represent as op = 'd' events; apply as DELETE or soft delete in silver
Schema change in the source table Bronze accepts it (raw payload or schema evolution); silver change goes through code review
Primary key updates Treat as delete of old key + insert of new key
Tombstone messages (null value) in Kafka Filter or interpret explicitly; do not let them fail the parser

8. Testing data pipelines

Level What it tests How
Unit tests Transformation functions on small in-memory DataFrames pytest with a local SparkSession or Databricks Connect; compare to expected DataFrames
Data tests Assumptions about real data: uniqueness, not-null, referential integrity, accepted values Expectations, dbt tests, SQL assertions in the pipeline
Integration tests The whole pipeline end to end on a representative dataset Deploy to a test environment with Asset Bundles; run the job; assert on outputs
Regression / reconciliation New code produces the same results as old for unchanged logic Run both versions on the same input; diff outputs with EXCEPT

Structure code so it is testable: pure functions from DataFrame to DataFrame, with I/O at the edges.

# transformations.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F, Window

def latest_per_key(df: DataFrame, key: str, order_col: str) -> DataFrame:
    w = Window.partitionBy(key).orderBy(F.col(order_col).desc())
    return df.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("_rn = 1").drop("_rn")

# test_transformations.py
import datetime as dt
import pytest
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual   # Spark 3.5+
from transformations import latest_per_key

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def spark():
    return SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").appName("tests").getOrCreate()

def test_latest_per_key_keeps_newest(spark):
    rows = [
        ("c1", "Leeds",   dt.datetime(2026, 1, 1)),
        ("c1", "Bristol", dt.datetime(2026, 6, 1)),
        ("c2", "York",    dt.datetime(2026, 3, 1)),
    ]
    df = spark.createDataFrame(rows, "customer_id string, city string, updated_at timestamp")

    result = latest_per_key(df, "customer_id", "updated_at")

    expected = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("c1", "Bristol", dt.datetime(2026, 6, 1)), ("c2", "York", dt.datetime(2026, 3, 1))],
        "customer_id string, city string, updated_at timestamp")
    assertDataFrameEqual(result, expected)

Test the awkward cases explicitly: nulls in keys, duplicate keys with identical timestamps, empty input, late records, schema with an extra column.

9. Environment promotion and CI/CD

---
title: CI/CD for a Databricks pipeline with Asset Bundles
---
flowchart LR
    PR["Pull request"] --> CI["CI: lint, unit tests,<br/>bundle validate"]
    CI --> DEV["Deploy to dev<br/>(per-user prefix)"]
    DEV --> MERGE["Merge to main"]
    MERGE --> TEST["Deploy to test<br/>run integration job"]
    TEST --> APPROVE{"Approval"}
    APPROVE --> PROD["Deploy to prod<br/>as service principal"]

Principles:

  • Same code, different configuration. Environment differences (catalog name, cluster size, schedule, notification targets) are bundle variables or job parameters, not code branches.
  • Catalog per environment (dev, test, prod), with code reading the catalog from a parameter: spark.table(f"{catalog}.silver.orders").
  • Nobody deploys to prod by hand. CI/CD deploys as a service principal, authenticated through workload identity federation rather than stored secrets where possible.
  • Test data: synthetic or masked extracts in test; never copy production PII into lower environments without masking.
  • Schema migrations (new columns, table property changes) are code-reviewed and deployed through the same pipeline, idempotently (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS guarded by a check).
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  deploy-prod:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod            # requires approval
    permissions:
      id-token: write            # for OIDC federation
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: databricks/setup-cli@main
      - run: databricks bundle deploy -t prod
        env:
          DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ vars.DATABRICKS_HOST }}
          DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID }}
          DATABRICKS_AUTH_TYPE: github-oidc

(Authentication settings depend on how federation is configured for your account; check the current Databricks CLI documentation for the exact variables.)

10. Cost optimisation

Lever Why it saves money
Job compute / serverless instead of all-purpose Lower DBU rate; nothing idles
Right-size clusters Look at CPU and memory utilisation in cluster metrics; many jobs are over-provisioned
Autoscaling (with sensible min/max) Pay for peak only during peak stages; avoid for streaming jobs where it causes churn
Spot / low-priority VMs for workers Large discounts on interruptible capacity; keep the driver on-demand; best for batch
Photon Faster SQL-heavy jobs can cost less overall despite a higher DBU rate — measure
availableNow instead of always-on streams Pay only while processing
File layout (clustering, compaction) Queries read less data → less compute
Incremental processing Process the day's data instead of all history
Auto-termination and auto-stop Idle interactive clusters and warehouses are pure waste
Cluster policies and tags Prevent oversized clusters; attribute spend to teams
Storage hygiene VACUUM, retention policies, delete abandoned tables and old checkpoints

Measure before and after: the system.billing.usage system table (joined with list prices) shows DBU consumption by job, cluster, warehouse and tag.

11. Performance tuning checklist

Work from the top: most wins come early.

  1. Read less data. Filter early; select only needed columns; make sure partition pruning and data skipping are happening (check files read vs pruned in the query profile).
  2. Fix the layout. Compact small files; cluster on common filter and join keys; avoid over-partitioning.
  3. Avoid unnecessary shuffles. Broadcast small dimensions; aggregate before joining; remove stray orderBy, distinct, repartition.
  4. Check skew. Max vs median task time; handle null keys; rely on AQE skew handling or salt.
  5. Right-size partitions. Let AQE coalesce; adjust spark.sql.shuffle.partitions for very large shuffles.
  6. Remove Python UDFs where built-in functions can do the job; use pandas UDFs where they cannot.
  7. Cache only what is reused, and unpersist.
  8. Use Photon for SQL/DataFrame-heavy workloads.
  9. Tune MERGE: deduplicate the source, add partition/cluster predicates to the ON clause, cluster the target on the merge key, enable deletion vectors.
  10. Choose instance types to match the bottleneck: memory-optimised for large joins and state, compute-optimised for CPU-bound parsing, storage-optimised for disk cache.

12. Common anti-patterns

Anti-pattern Why it hurts Instead
Business logic only in notebooks with no tests Fragile, unreviewable, copy-pasted Modules with unit tests, called from notebooks or wheels
now() inside transformations Non-reproducible reruns and backfills Logical date parameter
Blind append in re-runnable jobs Duplicates on every retry Merge or partition overwrite
Separate backfill scripts History diverges from daily logic One parameterised job
Partitioning by high-cardinality columns Millions of tiny files Liquid clustering
collect() / toPandas() on large data Driver out-of-memory Keep processing distributed; write results to tables
Schema inference on every run in silver Types change silently Explicit schemas; evolution only in bronze
One giant notebook doing ingest to gold A failure anywhere reruns everything Separate tasks per layer with dependencies
Dashboards querying bronze Wrong numbers, slow queries Serve from gold via SQL warehouses
Dropping bad rows silently Invisible data loss Quarantine with reasons and alerts
Personal credentials in jobs Breaks when people leave; audit gaps Service principals
No ownership on tables Nobody fixes problems Every table has an owning team in the catalog
Sharing checkpoints or deleting them casually Duplicates or data loss One checkpoint per query, versioned with the query
VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS to "save space" Breaks running readers and time travel Default retention, or a deliberate, reviewed exception

Azure / .NET mapping

Practice Azure / .NET tooling
CI/CD GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines running the Databricks CLI with bundles; Entra ID workload identity federation
Secrets Key Vault-backed secret scopes; no secrets in bundle YAML
Cost visibility Databricks system tables plus Azure Cost Management (VM and storage costs for classic compute)
Spot capacity Azure Spot VMs configured in cluster settings / policies
Testing mindset The same as xUnit for .NET: small pure functions, fixtures, explicit expected outputs — pytest plays the xUnit role
Calling pipelines from services .NET services trigger jobs via the Jobs REST API and poll run status, rather than embedding pipeline logic in the service

Review checklist

  • My incremental loads write data before advancing the watermark and tolerate overlap.
  • Every write in my pipeline is idempotent, and I can say which technique each uses.
  • I deduplicate within batches and against the target, with deterministic tie-breakers.
  • Late data has an explicit policy: watermark, rolling reprocessing window or correction job.
  • Backfills use the same parameterised job and replace exactly the slices they process.
  • I can build an SCD2 dimension from CDC and look up point-in-time surrogate keys.
  • CDC ingestion handles the initial snapshot, ordering, deletes and schema changes.
  • Transformations are pure functions with unit tests; pipelines have data tests and an integration run.
  • Deployments go through CI/CD to dev, test and prod with environment-specific configuration only.
  • I can name the top cost and performance levers and check them against a real job.
